title: NGC 4631: The Whale
caption: The Whale Galaxy (NGC 4631) and NGC 4627, imaged at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center
credit: KPNO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/John Vickery and Jim Matthes/Adam Block

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: NGC 4631, known as the Whale Galaxy, is a huge spiral galaxy that we see edge-on, so its disc appears as a long, narrow band. Astronomers class it as an Sc type spiral. Next to it lies a smaller companion, NGC 4627.

The companion seems to have bent the Whale slightly out of shape. Together, the two appear as entry Arp 281 in the Arp Catalog of Peculiar galaxies, and faint tidal tails can be traced between them. Tidal tails are streams of stars and gas pulled out when galaxies tug on one another with their gravity.

The Whale has another neighbor beyond the edge of this frame, to the southeast. That galaxy, NGC 4656, looks noticeably distorted, apparently from its own encounters with NGC 4631. Detailed surveys have found a thin bridge of hydrogen gas linking the two, a sign that they interacted in the past.
scale: This group of galaxies lies between 25 and 30 million light-years away, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light image taken with a CCD camera at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center's roll-off-roof observatory, using several broadband filters. The source does not say which color each filter was assigned.
